title: Col. John Todd of Lexington
summary: Lawyer John Todd (1750–1782) served Kentucky County, rode with George Rogers Clark, and became Fayette’s first militia colonel and a Lexington trustee.
bodyMarkdown:
[John Todd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Todd_%28Virginia_soldier%29) was born in Montgomery County, Pennsylvania, in March 1750. One account gives his birthday as March 27; [another gives March 20](https://uncommonwealth.lva.virginia.gov/blog/2021/01/06/23422/). Before he came west he served as adjutant to Andrew Lewis and fought at Point Pleasant in 1774.

## Into Kentucky

Todd [came to Kentucky in 1775](https://history.ky.gov/markers/county-named-1819-2) and settled in what became Fayette County. He soon represented Kentucky in the Virginia legislature. One account dates his first term to 1776, while [another places it in 1777](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/LegislativeMoments/moments09RS/web/Lincoln%20moments%2010.pdf). He also procured land grants for public schools and later introduced emancipation legislation in the Virginia House of Delegates. Todd also held people in slavery.

## Illinois County

Todd joined George Rogers Clark's 1778 expedition into the Illinois country. In December 1778 Virginia named him county lieutenant and civil commandant of the new Illinois County, an appointment made by Gov. Patrick Henry. He arrived at Kaskaskia in May 1779 and [resigned the post in 1780](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Journals/AHR/4/4/County_of_Illinois*.html), returning to Kentucky affairs. See also [George Rogers Clark](/stories/george-rogers-clark/).

## Lexington's colonel

Todd is counted among the founders of Lexington, alongside his brother [Levi Todd](/stories/levi-todd-lexington-co-founder/). The first blockhouse there went up in April 1779. In 1781 Todd [led the building of a stronger fort](https://history.ky.gov/markers/blockhouse-and-fort) 94 feet square, with rammed-earth walls seven feet thick meant to resist artillery. He married Jane Hawkins and became colonel of the Fayette County militia, with Daniel Boone serving as his lieutenant colonel.

## Blue Licks

In August 1782 a force of British rangers and Native warriors besieged [Bryan Station](/stories/bryan-station-siege-august-1782/), then withdrew north. Todd commanded the Kentucky militia that pursued them to the Licking River. The fight at [Blue Licks](/stories/battle-of-blue-licks/) was a severe defeat for the Kentuckians, and Todd was among those killed. Most accounts date the battle to August 19, 1782.

Levi Todd helped bury the dead days later. He wrote that the bodies had been stripped and that "our Brother was not known." John Todd was 32.

## Kentucky today

[Todd County](https://history.ky.gov/markers/county-named-1819-2), formed in 1819, carries his name. He was also a great-uncle of Mary Todd Lincoln, which ties the Lexington founder to a better-known family story. The site of his 1781 fort is marked in downtown Lexington.
